nv_black_orpheus_amphitheater.blurb: A big south-facing sandstone bowl in Oak Creek Canyon at Red Rock, tucked just upstream of Solar Slab. All 14 climbs here are trad, spread from easy fifth-class up through the 5.9 to 5.12 range, with a couple of much harder lines. The tall middle of the bowl holds the long multi-pitch classic that gives the place its name, while the left-hand Black Arch Wall offers shorter pitches and the right side is a southwest-facing alcove with mid-length lines. Expect a committing day on the longer routes, with rappels or a scramble to get down. Wet sandstone breaks easily, so wait for dry rock.

nv_thomas_creek.blurb: A small sport crag in the hills above Reno, at roughly 6,850 feet on the Sierra side of the Washoe basin. Fourteen bolted lines run from the high 5.8s to 5.12, with most of the weight on the 5.10 and 5.11 grades, so it suits someone warmed up on moderates who wants a short pumpy lap. The main wall has a roof or bulge to start, a broad ledge partway up, and a steep headwall above, and routes are short, around 45 feet on the right side. Some rock near the base is chossy. You cross the creek on a footbridge and follow cairns up the slope.

nv_winter_heat_wall.blurb: A dark, desert-varnished sandstone wall in the wash north of Kraft Mountain, in the Calico Basin part of Red Rock. Routes are a single pitch long and mostly trad, with two sport lines and one top-rope; the grade range runs from easy fourth class through the 5.7 to 5.12 bracket, with the bulk of the lines at 5.11. The namesake route is the area's best-known climb. The wall faces north to northeast, so it sits in shade through late fall and early winter and picks up morning sun in spring, then fades to little shade by early summer. Keep off it when the sandstone is damp.

nv_dali_dome.blurb: A quartz monzonite dome in the Christmas Tree Pass area of southern Nevada, with a rock quality often compared to Joshua Tree. Thirteen routes mix sport and trad, nearly all between easy terrain and 5.10: lots of slab climbing plus an excellent crack. Of the pass's crags, this one has the shortest walk in. The stone is solid but not very clean because few people climb here, and many of the bolts are old quarter-inch ones, so the bolted lines are runout rather than plush sport routes. Bring a trad rack, a cool head and a plan to check the hardware.

nv_the_cube.blurb: The first boulder you meet in the Kraft Boulders, near Calico Basin at Red Rock, and hard to miss. It is a tall sandstone block that makes every problem a highball, with an overhanging arete visible from the trail. The thirteen problems range from easy beginner lines on the west face, which also serve as the usual downclimbs, up to some of the area's hardest tests at V9 and beyond, so the choice of problems skews to either low grades or serious projects. The sunny side faces west. A bolt on top helps with rehearsing moves. Dry sandstone only.

nv_1_east_wall.blurb: The east-facing side of Owl Rock, a small desert sport crag near Reno. About a dozen bolted routes and one short boulder problem cover roughly 5.9 to 5.12, with most climbs in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, from short pumpy lines to longer moderates. The wall catches morning sun on cold spring and fall days and is valued mostly for its afternoon shade in summer. From the main trail you pass the fork for the north and west walls, then wrap around beyond a neighbouring wall to reach the base. Lowering anchors allow easy top-roping, and a helmet is wise because a few loose blocks remain.
